claim: Denning and Buzen 1978 (operational analysis, no assumption on the distribution of times): with M terminals of think time Z, queueing is certain past Mb* = (R0 + Z)/(Vb Sb) terminals, the saturation point, while visit ratios and mean service times do not change with N.

Sztrik (finite-source queue slides 2001 and book 2004, one server, citing Kleinrock vol. II sec. 4.12, not opened): the saturation number N* = (b + 1/λ)/b, b the mean service time and 1/λ a source's mean time before asking again, is where the light-load line E[T] = b meets the heavy-load line, and in a deterministic system it is the most sources that can be scheduled without mutual interference.

Lazowska, Zahorjan, Graham and Sevcik 1984, chapter 5: the asymptotic throughput bounds assume only that a customer's service demand at a centre does not depend on how many other customers are in the system, and the optimistic bound has a heavy-load and a light-load part that cross at one population.

Lazowska and others 1984, chapter 11: modelling n tightly coupled processors as one centre with service demands divided by n is a simple first cut that ignores that n processors can give significantly less than n times one processor's rate, and the real service rate rises with queue length until all processors are busy.
note: The collect file names the saved chapter but not its URL; the chapter 5 URL of c1-0302 is on the same site.

claim: Sztrik 2004 (book): the finite-source queue with N machines and r operators (r < N; exponential times between breakdowns and exponential repairs, one operator per machine, served in order of breakdown) is published exactly, with its steady-state probabilities and the mean down time and mean waiting time of a machine.

Choo 2016, quoting Hopp and Spearman's Factory Physics (1996, book not opened): critical WIP W0 = rb x T0 is the WIP that reaches the bottleneck rate at the raw process time with no variability; WIP above it adds only waiting, and with variability a WIP equal to W0 does not reach the maximum throughput.

Desruelle 1994 (IIASA working paper; one general single server with an infinite-server delay station): a two-moment approximation erred at most 15 % for service-to-delay ratios 0.1 to 4 with five customers, and with more customers its error grew, under 10 % below seven and under 20 % at fifteen.

Holtman and Gunther 2008: retrograde throughput is not possible in the standard machine-repairman model for any N, S or Z and is associated with load-dependent servers; synchronous queueing gives the worst-case throughput, a lower bound.

Gunther 2008 (arXiv 0808.1431): the Universal Scalability Law is proved equivalent to the synchronous throughput bound of a machine-repairman with state-dependent service rate, a worst-case lower bound, with Amdahl's law as a corollary.

Gunther 2011 (arXiv 1105.4301, memcached on one machine): a scalability fit needs at least half a dozen measured points and its predicted peak may lie outside any attainable configuration; after the cache lock was partitioned and statistics made per thread, the peak moved from 22 to 48 threads.

Suleman, Mutlu, Qureshi and Patt 2009 (ASPLOS; cycle-accurate simulation of 12 workloads at 1 to 32 threads): running critical sections on a faster core let MySQL keep speeding up to 32 threads where the symmetric chip saturated at 16, cut average execution time 34 % against an equal-area 32-core symmetric chip, and raised the saturating thread count in 7 of the 12 workloads.

Dorfman 1943 (pooled blood tests; independent items with one known rate p, exact tests, two rounds): pooling n items costs E(T)/N = 1/n + p' tests per item, p' being the chance a pool fails; the best pool is 11 at 1 % (80 % saved), 4 at 10 % (41 % saved) and 3 at 30 % (1 % saved), and the method needs a small rate and a group test cheaper than testing its members one by one.

Aldridge, Johnson and Scarlett 2019 (survey): Dorfman's scheme with pools of 3 beats one-by-one testing for p < 0.307 and a pool of 2 is never optimal; the 0.382 threshold is an asymptotic result for any adaptive scheme, not for a finite batch; in pandemic testing Dorfman was preferred partly for needing only two stages, PCR being slow.

Sobel and Groll 1959 (Bell System Technical Journal): when simultaneous tests run in stages of equal length, minimising the number of stages minimises the time, and the authors remark there may be some conflict with minimising the number of tests.

Najafi, Rigby and Shang 2019 (simulation over 9 months of three Ericsson projects; a failing batch is bisected; cost counted in test runs): batching saved 72 % of runs in project C (2.8 % culprits, most cost-effective batch 9) and 46 % in project A (2.4 times C's culprit rate, batch 4); with flaky tests counted C fell to batch 4 and 41 % (42 % in the abstract); maximum savings were 50, 47 and 74 % in the three projects.

Beheshtian 2020 (MSc thesis behind the TSE 2021 paper; simulation on nine open-source projects with failure rates under 25 %): five batching approaches saved 44 to 50 % of runs on average; Batch4 is a special case of Dorfman's method; on the projects with the highest failure rates, 22.51 and 19.36 %, the best batch was the smallest, four; owncloud, whose failures came in runs, had best batch 15 and 53 % saved.

Fallahzadeh, Bavand and Rigby 2023 (ESEC/FSE; replay on Ericsson and Chrome data, about 8.5 % of Chrome builds failing; a batch runs the union of the tests its changes request, and culprit search bisects down to four and reruns only failed tests): batching every waiting change kept the actual average feedback time with up to 91 % fewer machines (Chrome 36.48 minutes with 20 machines, 90.78 % fewer; Ericsson 8.33 hours with 5, 28.57 % fewer), while a fixed batch of 4 needed 8 machines at Ericsson (-14.29 %) and 61 at Chrome (71.89 % fewer).

Fallahzadeh, Rigby and Adams 2025 (replay of 285 million test results from Chrome, a Google project and JMRI; flaky failures non-blocking): batching cut median feedback time up to 99 % without missing a failure and selection up to 96 % while missing up to 55 % of failures; in larger projects with many concurrent builds batching gave the best feedback time, more so with few machines, while in the smaller JMRI with fewer concurrent builds a selection algorithm was fastest despite missing up to 55 % of failures, and where missed failures are intolerable the authors advise batching and prioritisation.

Mandarapu and Kunkunuru 2026 (preprint, not peer reviewed; a simulator and PostgreSQL; no failures modelled): flushing the instant the device is free with whatever has queued was within a median 0.1 % of the best oracle-tuned timer at loads above λ* = 2/F0, the batch settles at a fixed point, throughput is bounded by 1/δ, the added cost per record, and the closed-loop bound is conjectured, not proven.

PostgreSQL documentation (WAL settings, fetched 2026-11-19): commit_delay lets more transactions commit in one WAL flush only when load is high enough, applies only while at least commit_siblings other transactions are active, and defaults to zero (no delay).

DeWitt, Katz, Olken, Shapiro, Stonebraker and Wood 1984 (technical report of the SIGMOD paper; a back-of-envelope calculation): one log device allows at most 100 commits a second and committing 10 transactions per log write gives 1000, a commit group may commit only after the groups it depends on, and the notion of group commits 'appears to be part of the unwritten database folklore'.

Johnson, Pandis, Stoica, Athanassoulis and Ailamaki 2010 (VLDB, Aether; one machine, one TATP transaction, UpdateLocation): letting a thread detach from a transaction that waits for the log flush and run others (flush pipelining) gave the largest single gain, 68 % over the baseline, which the authors trace to relieving operating-system scheduler overload, and it depends on early lock release.

Gawlick and Kinkade 1985 (IMS/VS Fast Path, an experience report with no measurement): the log buffer is written when full, when a time limit expires or by normal processing, so a group of transactions commits at once, named Group Commit long after Fast Path was developed; a region hands its committing transaction to a dummy region and starts work on a new one.

Memon and others 2017 (Google, ICSE-SEIP, self-reported): testing every change made compute grow with the submission rate times the test pool; a milestone, cut about every 45 minutes at peak, runs the targets selected by reverse dependencies since the last one; passed to failed test targets per change are 99:1; and a simulation on one month found that running only targets within dependency distance 10 or 6 would save 42 or 55 % with no breakage missed, the cut chosen on the same data.

Ananthanarayanan and others 2019 (Uber, EuroSys, self-reported; replay of 9 months of one iOS monorepo): testing each change on top of those ahead of it kept P50 turnaround within 2.98x of an oracle where a single queue grew to 80x at 500 changes an hour, reached 1.2x with 500 build machines for 500 changes an hour, and rose 4x at P95 under contention; the main line, green 52 % of the time before, stayed green; real conflicts were 5 % between two concurrent changes touching the same parts and 40 % among 16.

Juloori and others 2025 (Uber, ICSE SEIP, self-reported; before and after a 21-week rollout in three monorepos of a strategy that added build-time prediction, priority for short builds and a speculation threshold, so not a test of the threshold alone): builds per change fell from 3.39 to 1.85 (Go), 4.93 to 2.57 (iOS) and 5.43 to 1.96 (Android), and CPU by 44.70, 34.86 and 52.23 %; GitHub's merge queue and GitLab's merge train speculate only the success paths, so after a failure later changes are retested, with delays when the failure rate is high.

Zuul documentation, Project Gating (fetched 2026-11-19, no figures): Zuul tests queued changes in parallel assuming all will pass and retests those behind a failed change without it, so at best as many changes as execution contexts are tested and merged at once and at worst one at a time; its window starts at twenty changes, grows by one per merge, halves per failure, and should be small when builds often fail.

GitHub documentation, Managing a merge queue (fetched 2026-11-19, no figures): each pull request is tested with the base branch and the pull requests ahead of it, build concurrency and merge limits each range from 1 to 100, merge limits carry a wait time and do not combine merge_group builds, and a setting lets a later passing group carry an earlier failing pull request for intermittent test failures.

Rust forge documentation (self-reported, no measurement): every pull request is tested after merge before it lands, which 'can scale poorly' with a CI run of about 3 hours, so small low-risk changes go in hand-built rollups, a failed rollup is rebuilt without the change its logs name, and massive rollups are rarely needed.

Gligoric, Eloussi and Marinov 2015 (Ekstazi, 615 revisions of 32 Java projects): selecting tests by recorded file dependencies cut end-to-end test time 32 % on average and 54 % for longer suites; on short suites the time ranged from 9 % to 138 % of running all tests, every slowdown being on short suites; it appears useful for suites over a minute.

Machalica, Samylkin, Porth and Chandra 2019 (Facebook, ICSE-SEIP, self-reported): predictive test selection halved the infrastructure cost of testing changes while still reporting over 95 % of individual test failures and over 99.9 % of faulty changes, selecting fewer than a third of the tests build dependencies select; it relies on later stages that run all tests, and training on flaky results gave very poor predictions.

Elbaum, Rothermel and Penix 2014 (30 days, 3.5 million suite runs of Google data): selecting suites by recent failure found 70 to 80 % of failing suites with failure window Wf = 96, about six times better than random selection of the same size.

Kondareddy, Azad, Singh and Henderson 2025 (Google, ICST, self-reported; replay of three months, post-submit): small frequent cycles of targets predicted to break cut the median time to detect a new breakage about 65 %, from 107 to 37 minutes, and with 25 % of targets reached 85 % recall.

Luo, Hariri, Eloussi and Marinov 2014 (201 commits likely fixing flaky tests in Apache projects): of the 161 classified fixes, 74 (45 %) were async wait, 32 (20 %) concurrency and 19 (12 %) test order; at Google (personal communication, self-reported) 4.56 % of 1.6 million test failures were flaky and a failing test is rerun 10 times.

Mossige, Gotlieb, Spieker, Meling and Carlsson 2017 (840 generated suites, test durations 1 to 800 s, shared resources and machine limits): assigning tests to machines at random was 30 to 60 % worse than a greedy assignment by known durations.
One run of the tree's test suite (1,018 tests) took 596 s with one test file at a time; it was one run, with other programs running.

The lane runs every heavy command through one queue whose slot count, 2, is read from capacity.txt (default 1, at most 4); over the 780 commands finished by 03:20 on 2026-11-18 they ran 365 minutes and waited about 177, and two ran at once in 41 of the 324 minutes any ran, never three.
Over 25 recorded episodes of our own work, the serial queue at heavy commands was the most frequent limit, named in 9.

The lane log carries the wait on every start line and the run time on every end line, but a queued command leaves no line until it starts or gives up and no line carries the slot count, so one slot against two cannot be compared from the log.

The lane kills a command at its timeout, which is capped at 1,500 s (25 minutes), and lets a waiter break a live holder's slot once the hold is 20 minutes old (no heartbeat), so a check of about an hour cannot run through today's lane.

When capacity.txt is lowered the lane tries only the slots below the new count, so a holder of a higher slot is not counted, and its break of a stale slot has no fence, so two waiters can break one slot twice.
Waiters at the lane have no order today; the build-in design, not built, would give a free slot to the shortest expected check, then the oldest, with an age cap.

The tree's checker batch is due at 12 candidates, a number marked 'guess' in thresholds.json, or when nothing else runs; check-queue orders its items by field and card id, not by age, and its ledger line carries no waiting time.
In the tree the coordinator may run only node tcb/<name>.mjs, so the lane is refused there.

The decision rule's case B is 'slots x (time outside + time inside) / time inside', marked 'a textbook queueing bound, reasoned', and the build-in design runs a check per merge, 596 s per suite run, with check width = the lane's 2 slots.
The decision rule's answer still lists 'a check shared by separate programs' among the parts with no paper among those read.

II, Reiser and Lavenberg 1980, Adams, Balas and Zawack 1988, Duclos and Spencer 1995, the TSE 2021 and ICSME 2021 batching papers, Hwang 1972, Deb and Serfozo 1973, Stecke and Aronson 1985, or the Hopp and Spearman and Goldratt books.

The lane check's 66 claims were folded as 41 confirmed, 23 holding in part, 2 refuted and 0 that cannot be checked; refuted and not to be proposed again: C44, that BMW keeps the full suite at its merge gate (its gate runs the same Bazel-affected targets as its pre-submit pipeline and leaves out only its history-based selection, as a fail-safe), and C64, that a session's rerun nondeterminism shrinks the best batch toward 2 to 4 (a split reruns the same merged code, so a failure that does not reproduce comes from flaky tests or changes failing together, and 2 to 4 has no source).

Untested and stated in no source read for c > 1: workers sharing c equal check slots reach the check's throughput cap at N* = c (S + Z)/S (S one check run, Z a worker's own time between checks), not 1 + cZ/S, which is c − 1 lower; it is computed on Sztrik's exact M/M/c//N model in 16 cases (c 1 to 4, Z/S 0.5 to 10) and follows for any time distribution from X <= c/S and X <= N/(S + Z), assuming S and Z do not change with N and the c slots run side by side at full speed, which is not measured on this PC.

Untested: at N = c (S + Z)/S the exponential M/M/c//N model already queues, the check 79 to 84 % busy for one slot and 85 to 92 % for 2 to 4 with mean waits of 0.16 to 2.15 check times (Z/S 1 to 10), so the cap is where two bounds cross, not where waiting starts; a near-fixed suite waits less, not zero.

Untested: batching k changes per run raises the check's throughput cap from c/S to c/(S C), C = 1/k + 1 − (1 − p)^k runs per change under Dorfman (5.0 times at p = 1 %, 1.7 at 10 %, 1.01 at 30 %), and c (S + Z)/(S C) is where that cap meets the light-load bound, reached only where full batches form; a greedy batch capped at k fits it and a fixed k that must first gather does not, and it assumes a run over k changes costs one run and independent failures.

Untested design, ranked first for our check: shorten each run (test files side by side, 596 s toward the longest file of about 270 s if the files are independent; selection by changed files in the builder's pre-check; at the gate the full suite until a dependency map exists, then the dependency-selected targets as BMW's gate runs, never prediction-based selection), which raises the cap by S/S' at every worker count; set by the suite time with files side by side, whether two runs at once slow each other, and the share of changes that select every file.

Untested design, ranked second: when a slot frees, run every waiting change together, capped by the measured failure rate (no batching near 30 % failing), and on a failure split the batch one by one when it fits the free slots, otherwise by halving; it costs nothing when one change waits and pays only where changes wait, by C runs per change while the gate runs the full suite (a selecting gate runs the union of the batch's selections); set by the failure rate per change at the gate, suite time on merges of 1, 2 and 4 changes, the share of batch failures whose changes each pass alone, and the flaky share of our tests.

Untested design, ranked third: if the gate tests each change on the main line with the changes ahead of it, test the next waiting change on top of an unfinished one in a free slot, on the success path only, with a window halved on each failure, since a speculative run whose base passes is the real check and is how a serial gate uses its second slot; it wastes runs in proportion to the failure rate and the depth, and is set by the failure rate per change and the window.
note: BUILD-IN.md section 1 does not say whether two merges checked at once share one base; checking them on one base accepts failures caused by two changes together.

claim: Untested design, ranked fourth: let a worker start its next unit while its change waits at the check, with a limit on its changes in flight and a way back for a failed one, because detaching removes the closed loop's own flow control and a late failure invalidates stacked work that costs tokens to redo; it saves clock time, not tokens, no measured gain carries over, and it is set by the share of a worker's cycle spent waiting at the check and the tokens of a redone unit.

Untested design, ranked fifth: log the slot count and the number waiting, give a free slot to the shortest expected check then the oldest, and set the lane's timeout cap and hold-break age above the longest check; it gains nothing by itself but makes the queue measurable and lets a check over 25 minutes run.

Untested design, ranked sixth: start no worker past c (S + Z)/S, or past c (S + Z)/(S C) once batching runs, and fewer where waits must stay short, since waiting starts below that point; set by the mean and spread of S, Z per change, the failure rate p, and whether runs side by side slow each other.

proposed correction of o1-0402: for one slot (T_out + T_check)/T_check is published (Denning and Buzen 1978; Lazowska 1984 ch. 5; Kleinrock via Sztrik), for c slots c (T_out + T_check)/T_check is computed on the exact model and follows from two operational bounds for any distribution, and it is where bounds cross, not where waiting starts; the same mark 'reasoned' stands on DECISION-RULE.md line 74 and BUILD-IN.md line 110.

proposed correction of x15-0405: the condition is Dorfman's 1943 published result, not reasoning, and its threshold depends on the pool: pools of 3 beat one-by-one testing below p = 0.307, a pool of 2 is never optimal, and the best pool at 1 % failing is 11.

proposed correction of x15-0406: (1 − p)^k > 1/k is Dorfman's 1943 cost condition (1/k + 1 − (1 − p)^k below 1 test per item), published with its table of best pools (11 at 1 %, 4 at 10 %, 3 at 30 %), and a batch of 2 is never optimal (Aldridge and others 2019).

proposed correction of x06-0404: batching losing at a high failure rate has published numbers: Dorfman's best pool saves 1 % at 30 % failing, Najafi's Ericsson project with 2.4 times the culprit rate saved 46 % at batch 4 against 72 % at batch 9, and the thesis behind TSE 2021 left out projects over 25 % failing and found the smallest best batch, four, at 19.36 and 22.51 %.
